newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl, SPD to hold make-or-break German tax summit.
newsitem.headline: Kohl, SPD to hold make-or-break German tax summit.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl meets opposition leader Oskar Lafontaine next Monday for talks which could make or break coalition tax reforms aimed at beating record unemployment and readying Germany for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Shaken by January's half-million surge in unemployment to 4.7 million -- the highest since 1933 -- both sides say they are ready to end a standoff and search for a quick deal to avert long and bitter wrangling in parliament.

But, with a general election looming in 1998, it remains unclear how far Social Democrat (SPD) leader Lafontaine will go to meet Finance Minister Theo Waigel's goal of cutting 30 billion marks ($17.8 billion) in taxes.
Thursday's parliamentary debate on the economy provided a mixed reading of SPD intentions.
Parliament leader Rudolf Scharping called for Kohl to resign at once, mocking his coalition's "meaningless promises and false starts".
Gerhard Schroeder, SPD premier of Lower Saxony state, struck a more conciliatory note, saying the opposition wanted to help Waigel pass reforms "but not at the price he has set".
Although Schroeder regularly outscores Lafontaine as the public's favoured SPD challenger to become chancellor next year, he will not join the first round of talks here on Monday.
By then Lafontaine -- also Saarland state premier -- will have recovered from a cold that sidelined him this week and will take a 10-point shopping list of demands into the talks.
Waigel's strategy plans a two-stage reform, with cuts in corporate taxes starting in 1998 and a drop in income tax in 1999. The cuts would be offset by scrapping 70 tax breaks.
Although no breakthroughs are expected at Monday's talks, which will start at 1400 GMT, compromises should be easy to reach on a bottom rate for income tax and on cutting corporate taxes.
Waigel's income tax model sees an entry bracket of 15 percent, down from 26 percent, with a sliding scale from 22.5 to 39 percent. The SPD wants a bottom rate below 20 percent.

But the top rate is problematic. The SPD is resisting a cut to 39 percent from 53 percent sought by Waigel -- but also realises that if income and corporate taxes are too far out of line, that could violate the constitution.
The SPD also wants tax relief to stay on night, weekend and holiday shifts -- which Waigel wants to abolish -- and rejects a rise in value-added tax to finance direct tax cuts.
Government spokesman Peter Hausmann said on Friday that the coalition was confident of winning the argument on tax reforms.
"We are optimistic our concept, which is well known and is on the table, will prevail," he told reporters.

The biggest barrier could be timing. Waigel wants most of the tax cuts to take effect in 1999 but the SPD and junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) are clamouring for bigger tax cuts in 1998.
Whether struggling state finances can cope with the extra cuts in 1998, on top of an already-planned reduction in the so-called solidarity surcharge on income tax, is doubtful.
Waigel admitted on Thursday he could only meet his 1997 budget deficit target of 2.9 percent of gross domestic product if savings measures blocked by the SPD in the Bundesrat upper house were passed.

Kohl said on Friday that Germany and other European states would have to make great efforts to qualify for EMU and a senior central banker said Germany might this year miss the three percent deficit goal set by EMU's guiding Maastricht treaty.
But Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke told the Frankfurter Rundschau Bonn would still join EMU's 1999 start.
Newspaper commentators have speculated that the cross-party talks could mark the prelude to a grand coalition between the Christian Democrats and the SPD.
But, according to Wirtschaftswoche magazine, Waigel is taking nothing for granted. Citing government sources, it said Waigel believed Lafontaine was following a two-prong strategy.

"In public he supports the euro but in the Bundesrat he is doing everything possible to thwart the attainment of the Maastricht criteria. The goal of the Saarland strategist: If EMU fails, then Kohl has to go," the magazine said.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49-228-26097 150 ($ = 1.685 German Marks)
